screens.title: Configuring Basic eBGP Peering on Junos
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to configure a basic external BGP peering between two Juniper routers. We start by establishing the router’s Autonomous System number under routing-options, then create a BGP group set to type external, and point each router to the other’s IP address with the correct peer-as. You’ll see concrete Junos configuration snippets for both sides of a direct point-to-point link and learn the verification commands you use to confirm the session reached Established. We’ll also walk through the most common mistakes that prevent a session from forming: IP reachability failures, AS number mismatches, blocked TCP 179, and incorrect source interfaces. Finally I’ll explain why these steps matter for connecting your network to an ISP or partner and how to safely test changes in a lab before applying them in production. By the end you’ll understand the minimal, correct configuration needed for eBGP and the quick operational checks that prove the session is healthy.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Configuring Basic eBGP Peering
Configuring Basic eBGP Peering on Junos
A compact, step-by-step orientation: local AS, external BGP group, neighbor and peer-as, verification, and troubleshooting.
In this lesson
Define local AS
routing-options autonomous-system
Coming up
Create external group
type external + neighbor peer-as
Goal
Reach Established state
show bgp summary
Why this matters

BGP is how autonomous systems exchange routing information. A single misconfigured AS number or blocked TCP 179 can prevent the session from forming and cause service disruptions. These basics protect your network from routing blackholes and accidental leaks when connecting to an ISP or partner.

Visual
AS number → BGP group → neighbor
Starter tip

Always configure the local autonomous-system before defining BGP groups. It’s required for BGP to run on Junos.

eBGP group & neighbor

screens.title: Autonomous System (AS) Number on Junos
screens.narratorSegment: An Autonomous System number uniquely identifies your routing domain to other BGP speakers. On Junos you declare this identifier under routing-options using the command set routing-options autonomous-system. This configuration is mandatory before BGP will operate on the device. Practically, think of the AS number as your network’s name on the global BGP stage — peers use it during the BGP open exchange to verify who they’re talking to. A concrete example from the chapter: if your enterprise uses AS 65001, you would run set routing-options autonomous-system 65001 and commit. A common misconception is that BGP can be configured entirely under protocols bgp without setting the local AS; however Junos requires the routing-options entry and will not complete the BGP FSM without it. Another point to note is that this AS value is local configuration and must match the communicating topology plan; it is not the peer-as. Key verification includes checking the committed configuration and ensuring that after configuring the AS you can create BGP groups that reference remote peer-as values. Takeaway: always set and verify the local AS before progressing to neighbor configuration — it prevents confusing failures later.

keyIdea.title: Set local AS first
keyIdea.text: Without routing-options autonomous-system set, Junos will not bring up BGP sessions. It is the foundational identifier for all BGP configuration.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Autonomous System (AS) Number
Routing-options autonomous-system
Declare the router’s AS before configuring BGP groups and neighbors.
Definition

An Autonomous System (AS) number uniquely identifies your routing domain to remote BGP peers. Junos requires the local AS to be configured under routing-options; without it BGP cannot run.

Why it matters
  • It appears in BGP OPEN negotiation and identifies your network.
  • Peer AS values are compared to this local AS during session establishment checks.
  • Misconfiguration leads to sessions failing before routing exchange begins.
Common misconception

Do not assume protocols bgp entries are sufficient; routing-options autonomous-system must be present so the BGP FSM can proceed.

Concrete example
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.0.1/30
set routing-options autonomous-system 65001
Checklist
  • Apply the routing-options statement.
  • Confirm with show configuration or commit confirmation.
  • Only then create BGP groups and neighbors.
Key Takeaway

Set routing-options autonomous-system before any protocols bgp configuration to ensure BGP can start.

screens.title: BGP Group and type external
screens.narratorSegment: A BGP group in Junos is a logical container for neighbors that share common settings. For eBGP peerings, you set the group type to external using set protocols bgp group type external. This flag explicitly marks that the neighbors in the group are in a different AS. The group helps you avoid repeating shared parameters across multiple neighbor statements; it’s a configuration convenience that keeps your BGP stanza concise and consistent. For example, in a simple point-to-point peering the group holds the type and neighbor statements while each neighbor line includes the peer-as for the remote AS. A common misunderstanding is to use type internal or omit the type entirely; internal is for iBGP inside a single AS and will not behave correctly for eBGP. The group also becomes the place to set policies or import/export rules that apply to all contained neighbors. Remember: for eBGP, use type external and specify neighbor peer-as. That explicit pairing is how Junos knows this is an external neighbor relationship. BGP Group and type external means define a bgp group with type external to collect neighbors that belong to remote ases and share settings like export/import policies.. In practical terms, using a bgp group to simplify ebgp neighbor configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › BGP Group & type external
BGP group: simplify neighbor config
Group type external signals eBGP peers in different ASes.
What it does

A BGP group collects neighbor definitions and shared parameters such as type, graceful-restart settings, and common policies. For eBGP, set the group type to external so Junos treats the group’s neighbors as remote AS peers.

Why not internal

Type internal is for iBGP inside a single AS. Using internal for an external peering will misclassify the relationship and lead to incorrect behavior.

Rule
Set type external for eBGP
Tip
Use descriptive group names
Example: TO_ROUTER_B
Example configuration
set protocols bgp group TO_ROUTER_B type external
set protocols bgp group TO_ROUTER_B neighbor 10.0.0.2 peer-as 65002
Common mistake

Using type internal when peers reside in different ASes will prevent the expected eBGP behavior.

screens.title: Configuring Router A (AS 65001)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete configuration for Router A in AS 65001. The steps are straightforward: configure the physical interface and IP address for the point-to-point link, set the local autonomous-system under routing-options, create a BGP group with type external, then add the neighbor and peer-as pointing to Router B. This sequence ensures the router knows its AS and who it expects on the other end. Below is the exact Junos snippet from the lesson source. After committing, you should see the neighbor attempt to establish a session. A common misconception is to swap local AS and peer-as; on Router A we set the local AS to 65001 and peer-as to 65002. If the peer-as is wrong, the session will not reach Established. After applying this configuration, verify connectivity with show bgp summary and a ping to the neighbor IP to confirm IP reachability. content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Router A Configuration
Router A: AS 65001
Ensure interface and local AS are configured before adding BGP neighbors.
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.0.1/30
set routing-options autonomous-system 65001
set protocols bgp group TO_ROUTER_B type external
set protocols bgp group TO_ROUTER_B neighbor 10.0.0.2 peer-as 65002
Practical note

After commit, check that the interface is up and that you can ping 10.0.0.2. If ping fails, BGP will not progress beyond TCP connection attempts.

Check
Ping neighbor, then show bgp summary
Misstep
Swapping local and peer AS numbers causes session failures.
Example scenario

Router A is directly connected to Router B via a /30 link. Use the snippet above to configure the link and the eBGP group. After commit, observe the BGP FSM as it progresses toward Established.

Key Takeaway

Match neighbor IP and peer-as to the remote router’s configured address and AS; commit and verify reachability immediately.

screens.title: Configuring Router B (AS 65002)
screens.narratorSegment: Router B’s configuration mirrors Router A’s but with the AS values switched. For a direct eBGP peering you must ensure that Router B has its interface IP and local autonomous-system configured, and that its BGP group points back to Router A’s IP with peer-as set to Router A’s AS. Symmetry is critical: each side must list the other’s IP and AS as the neighbor and peer-as. The chapter supplies the exact snippet for Router B: set the interface to 10.0.0.2/30, set routing-options autonomous-system 65002, create a protocols bgp group with type external, and add neighbor 10.0.0.1 peer-as 65001. After committing these commands, both routers should try to establish a TCP session on port 179 and then proceed through the BGP finite state machine to Established if reachability and AS numbers are correct. A useful troubleshooting step is to intentionally swap the peer-as on one side to observe the resulting OpenSent/OpenConfirm messages, which usually indicate an AS mismatch. Fixing the peer-as will allow the session to recover to Established. Configuring Router B (AS 65002) means router b must configure the interface, local as, and a bgp group that references router a’s ip and as to achieve a successful ebgp session.. In practical terms, mirror configuration on the remote side and observe symmetry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Router B Configuration
Router B: AS 65002
Symmetry: each router points to the other's IP and AS.
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.0.2/30
set routing-options autonomous-system 65002
set protocols bgp group TO_ROUTER_A type external
set protocols bgp group TO_ROUTER_A neighbor 10.0.0.1 peer-as 65001
Verification tip

After commit, ping 10.0.0.1 from Router B. If ping is successful, proceed to show bgp summary. If ping fails, fix IP or interface issues first.

Check
Confirm peer-as matches the remote autonomous-system
Pitfall
Forgetting to set the local AS on Router B prevents proper identification
Scenario note

This mirrored configuration is typical for ISP or partner links and demonstrates the minimal set of commands required to create a functioning eBGP peering on Junos.

Key Takeaway

Both sides must reference the other’s IP and AS. Symmetry reduces configuration mistakes.

screens.title: Verify eBGP Peering with show bgp summary
screens.narratorSegment: Verifying the peer is essential after committing configuration. The primary operational command is show bgp summary, which gives an overview of all BGP groups and peers, their remote AS values, prefix counts, and most importantly their current state. You want to see the neighbor state transition to Established. The chapter shows example output where a neighbor entry lists its IP, AS, packet counters, last up/dwn, and the state column showing Establ. When troubleshooting, find the neighbor line and check if it says Active, OpenSent, or Established. Active typically means repeated TCP connection failures often due to IP reachability; OpenSent/OpenConfirm can indicate AS mismatches or capability negotiation problems. A concrete step: after committing on both routers, run show bgp summary on each router and compare the state field. If Established appears on both sides, exchange of routes can begin. As a closing check, if you see Established but no prefixes, verify route advertisement policies and that each side is actually configured to send routes into BGP. content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Verify with show bgp summary
Interpreting show bgp summary
A quick glance tells you the neighbor state and whether prefixes are being exchanged.
user@routerA> show bgp summary
Groups: 1 Peers: 1 Down peers: 0
Table          Tot Paths  Act Paths Suppressed    History Damp State    Pending
inet.0
             0          0          0          0          0          0
Peer                     AS      InPkt     OutPkt    OutQ   Flaps Last Up/Dwn State
10.0.0.2              65002        100        100       0       0 00:05:30 Establ
What to look for
  • State: Establ means the session is up.
  • Prefix counts: ensure In/Received numbers make sense.
  • Packet counters: confirm there is TCP activity between peers.
Troubleshooting hints
  • If state is Active, first test ICMP ping to the neighbor.
  • If state is OpenSent/OpenConfirm, validate peer-as values.
  • If Established but no prefixes, check advertisement policies.
Key Takeaway

show bgp summary is your first stop for BGP health. Interpret the State column to guide your next debug step.

screens.title: show bgp neighbor — Deep inspection
screens.narratorSegment: When show bgp summary indicates a problem or when you need details about the peer relationship, use show bgp neighbor. This command provides a deep view: negotiated capabilities, hold and keepalive timers, the exact FSM state, and message counters. It helps you diagnose why peers are not progressing — for example, mismatched capabilities or hold-time discrepancies can be spotted here. A practical example: if you suspect an AS mismatch, show bgp neighbor reveals the remote AS reported by the neighbor during OPEN exchange. If you see capability differences, you can decide whether to adjust local settings or accept the negotiated defaults. Another common use is to confirm which local interface the router uses to source the BGP session; if the source is wrong on devices with multiple interfaces, you can adjust configuration or add a session specific source-address. screens.title: Common eBGP Configuration Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: When an eBGP session fails, the cause is commonly one of a few predictable items. First, IP reachability: if routers cannot ping each other over the peering link, TCP on port 179 will never complete. The first check is a simple ping to the neighbor IP. Second, AS number mismatch: if peer-as does not match the neighbor’s configured autonomous-system, the session will fail during OPEN negotiation; use show bgp neighbor to confirm the remote AS. Third, firewall or ACL blocking: ensure TCP 179 is allowed between the peers. Fourth, incorrect source interface: on multi-homed devices BGP might source from an unexpected address; verify which local address is being used and adjust or bind the source if necessary. A common misconception is to assume BGP failures are always complex; often a single ping or a mistyped AS number is the root cause. A helpful troubleshooting order is PING first, then show bgp summary, then show bgp neighbor, and finally inspect ACLs and source addresses. This keeps your debugging efficient and avoids unnecessary changes in production. Lab scenario: R1 ↔ R2

Starter configuration templates

edit

Third, eBGP Type and Peer-AS: an external group plus neighbor peer-as explicitly pairs the local router with the remote AS for session establishment. Use these three items as a checklist whenever you build a new eBGP peering. They are minimal, but they are the ground truth for a functional session. Ask yourself: have I set the local AS, made an external group, and pointed the neighbor to the correct peer-as? If yes, proceed to verification.

Here are three operational reminders to use in the lab and in production. First, show bgp summary provides a quick health check including neighbor state and prefix counts; look for Established. Second, show bgp neighbor gives the full detail: remote AS, negotiated capabilities, timers, and source address information — this is your forensic command for session issues. Third, a concise troubleshooting checklist: Ping the neighbor to confirm IP reachability, verify peer-as values match the remote autonomous-system, and ensure TCP 179 is not blocked. If you follow this checklist in that order you will resolve the majority of eBGP failures quickly. Carry these commands and the PING → SUMMARY → NEIGHBOR → ACL flow with you when you debug a peering; they keep troubleshooting focused and efficient.
